sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`chan T` can send and receive, `chan<- T` is send-only, and `<-chan T` is receive-only. Direction is a compile-time restriction on how a function may use the channel value.

A bidirectional channel can be passed to a parameter with one direction. The function then receives only the capability it needs, and the compiler rejects operations in the wrong direction.

For example, a generator can return `<-chan int`, making callers consumers only. Inside, its producer goroutine sends values and closes the channel after the final value.

Direction does not prevent deadlock, guarantee a close, or make several senders agree on ownership. A nil channel still blocks forever on send or receive.

Expose a directional channel at API boundaries when a function owns only production or consumption. It documents ownership and prevents accidental sends, receives, or closes.

sections.title: The core model: directional channels in Go
sections.content:
directional channels in Go is easiest to understand by following the data or control from input to result. The details below form one connected model rather than a list of unrelated rules.

Directional types express capability rather than creating different channel objects. A function accepting `<-chan Job` cannot send jobs or close that parameter; a function accepting `chan<- Result` cannot receive results. This narrows the legal operations and makes a pipeline review easier.


sections.title: The practical decision: directional channels in Go
sections.content:
The useful question is not whether directional channels in Go can be used, but which requirement makes it the clearest and safest fit. That decision includes its cost and its failure boundary.

sections.title: Why the failure happens: directional channels in Go
sections.content:
Failures around directional channels in Go usually come from one incorrect assumption about ownership, state, ordering, or lifetime. Finding that assumption is more useful than adding a defensive line at random.

Closing announces that no future values will be sent; it is not a request for receivers to stop. The sender with knowledge of completion normally owns that announcement. Multiple producers need coordination so exactly one closer runs after all senders have finished.

sections.title: The important trade-off: directional channels in Go
sections.content:
directional channels in Go and exposing a bidirectional channel everywhere solve related problems, but they expose different guarantees. The best choice follows from the guarantee the program actually needs.

Directional channels improve the type contract but do not change buffering, synchronization, or scheduling. Converting a bidirectional value to a one-way capability is safe narrowing. Designing everything as bidirectional makes ownership implicit and lets accidental operations compile.

sections.title: A reliable diagnosis: directional channels in Go
sections.content:
A good investigation traces the first point where the real state differs from the expected state. With directional channels in Go, that means observing the relevant input, transition, and result rather than guessing from the final symptom.

A reliable pipeline must handle both normal completion and early cancellation. Each sending select can also observe `ctx.Done`, every output has one close owner, and the parent waits for started stages. A blocked stack trace then maps directly to a missing lifecycle rule.
